learn: A just-right book is one you can read with only a few tricky words on each page.
Try the five-finger test: read a page and put up a finger for each word you don't know. Zero or one finger is too easy. Two or three is just right. Five is too hard for now.
Reading just-right books every day makes you a stronger reader.
check: In the five-finger test, how many fingers means "just right"?
A few tricky words on each page
It makes you a stronger reader
It is a rule for grown-ups
lessons.try: Do the five-finger test on two books from your shelf.

learn: Reading stamina is how long you can read and stay focused.
Find a quiet spot, get comfortable and set a timer for ten or fifteen minutes.
Add a few more minutes each week. Your reading muscles grow like any muscle.
check: How long you can read and stay focused
Add a few more minutes each week
lessons.try: Read for 15 minutes without stopping. Write down the page you reached.

learn: Readers talk about books to understand them better.
You can share your favourite part, a question you have, or a connection to your own life.
A connection might be: "This reminds me of when I lost my dog."
check: Why do readers talk about books?
This reminds me of my trip
What can you share about a book?
lessons.try: Tell someone about a book you read this week and make one connection.

learn: Every vowel can make a short sound or a long sound.
A short vowel is often alone between consonants: hat, pet, sit, hop, cup.
A long vowel says its own name: hate, Pete, site, hope, cute.
check: Which word has a short vowel?
Which word has a long vowel?
lessons.try: Sort these words into short and long vowels: map, cake, fin, bike, rob, robe.

learn: A syllable is a word part with one vowel sound.
A closed syllable ends with a consonant, and the vowel is short: cat, rab-bit.
An open syllable ends with a vowel, and the vowel is long: me, go, ti-ger.
check: In a closed syllable, the vowel is usually...
lessons.try: Clap the syllables in tiger, rabbit and robot. Are they open or closed?

learn: Long vowels can be spelled in different ways.
Long a: cake, rain, play. Long e: me, feet, beach. Long o: home, boat, snow.
If you're not sure how to spell a word, try it more than one way and pick the one that looks right.
check: Which word spells long a with ay?
Which word spells long o with oa?
If you're not sure how to spell a long vowel word, you can...
lessons.try: Write three different words with long a, each spelled a different way.

learn: Some vowel pairs glide from one sound to another.
oi and oy say /oy/ as in coin and boy.
ou and ow say /ow/ as in cloud and cow.
check: What sound does oy make in "boy"?
lessons.try: Read: toy, soil, mouth, crown, point, shout.

learn: When r comes after a vowel, it changes the vowel's sound. This is a bossy r.
ar as in car and star. or as in fork and storm.
er, ir and ur all sound the same: her, bird, turn.
check: Which has the same sound as "bird"?
Why is it called a bossy r?
lessons.try: Read: farm, horn, fern, girl, burn, shark.

learn: oo can say /oo/ as in moon or the short sound in book.
Some words have silent letters: the k in knee, the w in write, the b in lamb.
Silent letters must be remembered, because you cannot hear them.
lessons.try: Read: spoon, foot, knock, wrap, thumb.

learn: Main characters are the most important people or animals in the story.
We learn about characters from what they say, do, think and feel.
Characters can change by the end of the story.
check: How do we learn about characters?
What they say, do, think and feel
The most important person in the story
lessons.try: Pick a character from a book and list three words that describe them.

learn: The setting is where and when the story happens.
Settings can be real places, like a city, or make-believe places, like a castle in the clouds.
Authors use describing words so you can picture the setting.
check: Where and when the story happens
Authors help you picture the setting with...
lessons.try: Draw the setting of your favourite story.

learn: The plot is what happens in the story.
Most plots have a problem that the characters try to solve.
In "The Three Little Pigs", the problem is the wolf. The solution is the brick house.
check: In "The Three Little Pigs", what is the problem?
What solves the problem in that story?
lessons.try: Name the problem and solution in a story you know.

learn: A fable is a short story, often with animals, that teaches a lesson called a moral.
In Aesop's "The Ant and the Grasshopper", the ant works all summer while the grasshopper plays. In winter, the ant has food.
The moral is: work hard now and be ready for later.
check: A short story that teaches a lesson
lessons.try: Retell "The Ant and the Grasshopper" and say its moral.

learn: Characters have feelings, just like real people.
Look for clue words like smiled, cried, stomped or trembled.
Their feelings can change when things happen.
lessons.try: Find three feeling clues in a story.

learn: Different characters can see the same event in different ways.
In "Goldilocks and the Three Bears", Goldilocks thinks she found a nice house. The bears think someone broke into their home.
Try reading a part aloud in a different voice for each character.
check: Do characters always see things the same way?
How did the bears feel about Goldilocks?
How can you show different characters when reading aloud?
Use a different voice for each
lessons.try: Retell Goldilocks from Baby Bear's point of view.

learn: Nonfiction books are made of paragraphs, and each paragraph has a main topic.
Often the first sentence tells you what the paragraph is about.
The other sentences give details.
check: Where is the main topic often found?
What do the other sentences give?
lessons.try: Read a paragraph in a nonfiction book and say its main topic.

learn: Nonfiction uses features to help readers find information.
Bold words are important. A glossary explains them. An index lists topics and their pages.
Diagrams show parts of something, with labels.
check: What lists topics and their pages?
lessons.try: Find the glossary and the index in a nonfiction book.

learn: Good readers ask questions before, during and after reading.
Who, what, where, when, why and how questions help you understand.
Look back in the text to find the answers.
check: Where do you find the answers?
lessons.try: Write two questions about a topic, then read to find the answers.

learn: A collective noun names a group: a flock of birds, a herd of cows, a team of players.
Some nouns have irregular plurals: one foot, two feet; one mouse, two mice; one tooth, two teeth.
These must be remembered.
check: A group of birds is a...
lessons.try: Write the plurals of man, goose and child.

learn: Many verbs add ed to show the past: walk, walked.
Irregular verbs change: sit, sat; run, ran; go, went; tell, told.
The verb must match when the action happened.
lessons.try: Write five sentences about yesterday using past tense verbs.

learn: Adjectives describe nouns: a tall tree, a soft blanket.
Adverbs describe verbs, often telling how: she ran quickly, he spoke softly.
Many adverbs end in ly.
lessons.try: Add an adjective and an adverb to: "The dog barked."

learn: A complete sentence has a subject (who or what) and a predicate (what they do or are).
"The frog jumped" is complete. "The frog" is not.
Fix incomplete sentences by adding the missing part.
lessons.try: Make "Ran to the park." into a complete sentence.

learn: You can join two short sentences with and, but, or, or so.
"I like apples. I like pears." becomes "I like apples and pears."
"It rained. We stayed inside." becomes "It rained, so we stayed inside."
check: "I like apples and pears" joins two ideas with...
"It rained, so we stayed inside" shows...
lessons.try: Join these: "I was hungry. I ate a snack."

learn: Capitalise names, places, days, months and holidays: Monday, July, Texas.
Use commas in dates (July 4, 1776) and in a greeting of a letter (Dear Sam,).
An apostrophe can join two words (do not becomes don't) or show who owns something (the dog's bone).
check: The bone belongs to the dog
lessons.try: Write today's date with a comma and one sentence with an apostrophe.

learn: Before writing, plan your characters, setting and problem.
A story map has boxes for beginning, middle and end.
Planning helps you know where your story is going.
check: What should you plan before writing?
A story map has boxes for...
Know where your story is going
lessons.try: Fill in a story map for a new story.

learn: Details help readers see, hear and feel your story.
Dialogue is what characters say. Put the words they say inside quotation marks: "Help!" yelled Max.
Strong verbs like dashed or whispered are better than plain verbs like went or said.
check: Where do the spoken words go?
lessons.try: Add one line of dialogue and one strong verb to your story.

learn: Revising means making your writing better: adding details, changing words or moving parts.
Editing means fixing capitals, punctuation and spelling.
Read your story aloud. It helps you hear what to fix.
check: What helps you hear what to fix?
lessons.try: Revise one part of your story and edit it for capitals and periods.

learn: In opinion writing, state your opinion, give reasons, and end with a conclusion.
Use linking words like because, also and for example.
"Recess should be longer because exercise helps us learn. Also, we can make friends."
check: What comes first in opinion writing?
What do you give to support an opinion?
lessons.try: Write an opinion paragraph about the best season, with two reasons.

learn: A friendly letter has a date, a greeting, a body, a closing and a signature.
The greeting starts with "Dear" and ends with a comma: Dear Grandma,
The closing might be "Love," or "Your friend," followed by your name.
lessons.try: Write a friendly letter to someone in your family.

learn: Research means finding facts about a topic.
Use books, trusted websites or ask an expert, like a librarian.
Take notes in your own words and write down where you found each fact.
lessons.try: Research an animal and write three facts with where you found them.
